title: The Throne verse
hook: the Living, the Sustainer, whose Throne extends over heavens and earth, who never tires of guarding them (2:255)

segments.voice: Yesterday: what they ask about, and your line, good for them is best. Did you ask whether something was good for someone in your care? Today, the verse many Muslims call the greatest. Day three hundred fifty-six.

Count what you're guarding right now. Your phone's battery. A child's fever, or a parent's appointments. The inbox. The rent. The plant on the windowsill you keep forgetting. Most of us guard a dozen things at once, and by evening we're tired from it, sometimes too tired to sleep. Last year you heard the story of Ayat al-Kursi and the names inside it. This year we read it the way al-Baqarah places it, line by line, and end on its last picture: guarding without tiring. Today: the Throne verse.
screen: `COUNT WHAT YOU'RE GUARDING.` → `TIRED BY EVENING.` → `GUARDING WITHOUT TIRING.`

segments.voice: Read the verse just before it first. Verse two hundred fifty-four warns of a day when there's no trading, no friendship and no intercession. Every human safety net, gone. Then verse two hundred fifty-five answers: here is who holds everything when those are gone. In Pickthall's words: “Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him.” Then it widens, step by step. Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him. Who could intercede with Him, except by His permission? So the intercession that verse two fifty-four took away comes back, but only through Him. He knows what's before people and what's behind them, and they grasp nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. Then the picture that names the verse: “His throne includeth the heavens and the earth, and He is never weary of preserving them.” The Arabic for never weary is la ya'uduhu: it doesn't weigh on Him, doesn't bend Him under the load. The word is used for a branch sagging under weight. Everything you're guarding, and everything everyone is guarding, the whole sky and earth, doesn't make Him sag. And the last line: “He is the Sublime, the Tremendous.” Many Muslims recite this verse after each obligatory prayer and before sleep. Notice why the bedtime habit fits. You lie down still guarding: the phone, the child, the rent. The verse hands the watch to someone who doesn't sleep and doesn't tire, so you can. He never tires.
screen: `NO TRADE, NO FRIEND, NO INTERCESSOR` · `THE ALIVE, WHO NEVER SLEEPS` · `ONLY BY HIS PERMISSION` · `LA YA'UDUHU: IT DOESN'T WEIGH ON HIM`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite it once, understanding each line. If you know it in Arabic, say it slowly, and after each sentence, pause and recall what it means. If you don't, read it in English, one sentence per breath: the Alive, the Eternal; no slumber, no sleep; everything belongs to Him; no one intercedes but by His leave; He knows before and behind; His throne includes heavens and earth; guarding them doesn't tire Him; the Sublime, the Tremendous. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
The Throne verse. Ayat al-Kursi, al-Baqarah 2:255: the Alive, who never sleeps, whose throne includes heavens and earth, and who never tires of guarding them. Today's word.
Your line: he never tires. Tonight, before sleep, name one thing you're tired of guarding, and set it down. Day three hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi after each obligatory prayer, before sleep, and when leaving home, and children often learn it early as a verse of protection.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse of protection.
what it means: a portrait of the one who holds everything, read right after a warning that every human safety net will fail.
what a scholar hears: la ya'uduhu, from a root for bending under a load: guarding all of heaven and earth doesn't make Him sag.
